content:
Apple has asked the court hearing its lawsuit against OpenAI and other defendants to allow its own experts to review the forensic image files used in the case, and to also obtain documents related to OpenAI's hardware development. Here are the details.

A bit of background

In early July of this year, Apple sued former employees, OpenAI, and io Products, accusing them of misappropriating trade secrets.

The lawsuit involves former Apple employees who are alleged to have taken confidential materials with them when they left. Apple alleged that former employee Chang Liu provided coaching advice to another Apple staffer ahead of an OpenAI interview, while Tang Tan instructed people applying for Apple positions to bring hardware components and other materials to interviews.

Earlier, Apple said preliminary forensic examination showed that the MacBook Liu used after leaving the company had been used during his time at OpenAI to run a simulation involving a confidential Apple circuit diagram. Apple also said the MacBook indicated Liu had used a Mac mini, and the company has since sought access to that device in the case.

OpenAI subsequently pushed back against Apple's claims, arguing that the situation was "Apple's own doing," because Apple's claimed offboarding and security procedures were lax, allowing employees to inadvertently retain access to confidential information after they left.

One point of dispute in the case is Apple's request to expedite discovery, which OpenAI opposes. Another is Apple's motion for an injunction that would, during the pendency of the lawsuit, restrict OpenAI's use of the trade secrets it allegedly misappropriated — a move that could affect OpenAI's ongoing hardware development work.

Apple argues that, because OpenAI is still developing hardware products, it is necessary to expedite certain discovery, since any alleged use of Apple trade secrets could become further commingled with that product development, making it increasingly difficult to reconstruct.

OpenAI countered that Apple has not explained why a separate expedited discovery procedure is needed, and said Apple's requests are overly broad.

With the parties at an impasse, the court ordered them to submit a joint letter outlining their respective positions on expedited discovery. That letter was filed last Friday and has since been unsealed.

Apple seeks forensic images and development records

In the joint letter, Apple asked the court to allow its own forensic expert to directly review the raw forensic image files that the defendants' experts relied upon to analyze Liu's devices and determine whether he accessed or used Apple confidential information after his departure.

Apple said one of its forensic experts had identified what it called "significant flaws" in that analysis, and argued that its expert needed direct access to determine whether there were additional problems with the defendants' forensic analysis.

Here is Apple's statement:

Apple's forensic expert has identified multiple significant flaws in the defendants' experts' analysis, including: (1) failure to locate files that were evidently used and stored on Liu's Mac mini; and (2) erroneously concluding that files on the Mac mini with a size of zero bytes or an empty kMDItemLastUsedDate field had never been accessed. […] Allowing Apple's expert direct access to these forensic images is critical to understanding what other errors the defendants' experts may have made.

OpenAI argued that Apple's expert should not be given unrestricted access to the forensic images, and proposed instead that a neutral forensic expert handle them under a procedure agreed upon by both sides.

Apple countered that such an arrangement would put it at a disadvantage, because the defendants' own forensic experts already have direct access to the same material.

Beyond the forensic material, Apple is also seeking expedited production of documents related to OpenAI's hardware development, including work on metal finishing, power management, and battery functionality.

OpenAI had earlier argued that its metal finishing technology was independently developed and did not use Apple's confidential information, and that the simulations Liu ran using Apple confidential files had nothing to do with its upcoming products.

Apple is now asking for the underlying development records to verify those claims; OpenAI says this is merely an attempt to "spy on a competitor."

The joint letter also addressed a number of other points of dispute, including:

  • Apple's broader request for forensic images from devices currently or formerly used by Liu, Tan, former Apple employee Yu-Ting "Alyssa" Peng, and another OpenAI employee, where those devices contained or had contained what Apple defined as "Apple-derived information";
  • Records of Liu's use of AI tools — the defendants had previously said the forensic investigation found no evidence he used Apple confidential files with platforms including ChatGPT, Codex, Claude, or OpenClaw;
  • Interview-related documents from OpenAI's consumer hardware product division, including what materials were actually used during interviews, and communications with departing Apple employees;
  • OpenAI said that some of these interrogatories could affect more than 400 former Apple employees currently working at the company.

Apple is also seeking the complete LINE conversations between Liu and Peng, including messages in which Peng asked Liu technical questions about his Apple work after Liu had left the company.

The defendants, in opposing Apple's injunction motion, had submitted selected excerpts of those conversations, but Apple argues it should be permitted to review the full exchanges rather than only the portions defendants submitted.
